text: Anthropic filed its S-1 on October 26. It is the first public look at the company's finances. Hover or tap any chart for exact numbers. A year ago Anthropic was doing under $1B a quarter. Now it's doing $11.6B, and the last quarter alone was more than double the one before. Quarterly revenue 30.7 × in five quarters $41M of revenue in all of 2023, $386M in 2024, $4.6B in 2025. The first six months of 2026 brought in more than three times all of last year. The usual worry about AI labs is that every dollar of revenue costs more than a dollar of compute. Chips and data centers are expensive, and the more people use the product, the more you spend. That was true here until this year. Below the dashed line, compute cost more than it brought in. Revenue per $1 of compute expense Sub- $1 through 2025; above break-even from Q1 2026. Revenue grew far faster than the compute bill. Indexed growth, Q2 2025 = 1× Revenue 14.7 × , compute 4.0 × Each new dollar of revenue cost less to serve than the last, which is called operating leverage. Q2 2026 ended with $974M of operating profit, the company's first profitable quarter. The compute line also includes training new models, so the margin on serving customers is higher than this chart shows. Over the full first half, costs were still slightly ahead of revenue. Where the money went, first half of 2026 $16.3B in, $17.0B out. Compute: 53 % of costs. Scroll sideways → About 80% of revenue is usage-based: businesses call Claude through the API and pay by the token, like a utility bill. Compute eats more than half of all spending. The thin red band is the $693M gap, which Anthropic paid from cash. Most of the $80.7B net loss is an accounting entry. How the $80.7B loss adds up 90 % is an accounting entry. No cash moved. Almost all of it is one line: a "fair-value remeasurement." Some early investors put money in through convertible notes and SAFEs, which are IOUs that turn into shares later. When Anthropic's valuation shot up, those IOUs became worth a lot more, and accounting rules make the company book that increase as a loss. No cash moved. Operating cash flow was about $3.9B positive, and Anthropic held $131.7B of cash and investments in June. The number of customers spending $100K+ a year rose more than 12× in twelve months. Customers with $100K+ trailing-12-month spend 12.5 × YoY At the top, about 250 customers each spend $10M or more a year. Customer tiers by trailing-12-month spend Nested; area to scale. Net revenue retention was about 900%. That means the average business customer spent nine times more this year than last. Revenue is also concentrated. Who pays, and how (each square = 1% of revenue) Three cuts of H1 2026 revenue. 80 % usage-based 48 % via hyperscaler marketplaces 20 % from the top two customers Almost half comes through Amazon, Google and Microsoft's cloud marketplaces, and all three also build competing models. A fifth comes from just two customers. The S-1 says that share is shrinking. Compute commitments by counterparty ≈$ 637 B aggregate. Blue: H1 2026 revenue. Anthropic has signed deals with seven companies for chips, data centers and cloud capacity, worth roughly $637B in total. That's 39 times what it made in the first half of the year. Not all of it is locked in. Some amounts are ceilings and some deals can be canceled. But the part Anthropic must pay no matter what was $265.6B as of June, and most of it runs to 2033 or later. The bill vs. the bank account The must-pay part alone is 2.0 × the cash. Area to scale. The costs are fixed for years. The revenue is mostly pay-as-you-go, and customers can cut back any month. If demand slows, the contract payments do not. The risk factors run more than 90 pages, about a quarter of the filing. Anthropic writes that its models "may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways" and mentions "catastrophic or existential" risks that insurers might not cover.
